title: Internal resistance and terminal potential difference

learning_outcomes.text: understand the effects of the internal resistance of a source of e.m.f. on the terminal potential difference

external_knowledge: Topic 9: use V = IR and P = VI for a resistor.
Lesson 1: read a simple one-loop circuit diagram.

prior_knowledge_summary: Lesson 2 established e.m.f. as source energy supplied per unit charge and potential difference as energy transferred per unit charge.
Lesson 2 established that an ideal source has no internal energy transfer.
Topic 9 supplied V = IR and P = VI.
new_learning: Model a real source as an e.m.f. in series with internal resistance r.
Interpret Ir as lost volts and use V = 𝓔 - Ir.
Explain how changing current changes terminal potential difference and output power in a simple external load.
Determine internal resistance from e.m.f., current and terminal potential difference.
not_yet_taught: Kirchhoff's second law as a general loop method

demand_inventory: explain terminal-p.d. change when current changes
connect current change to source power

visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch with sparse labels

blocks.heading: Why does the battery voltage sag?
content: A fresh 6.0 V battery reads close to 6.0 V when almost no current is drawn. Connect a demanding motor and the reading across the same battery falls. The source has not suddenly changed its e.m.f. What inside the battery accounts for the missing energy per coulomb?
Predict what happens to the terminal reading when the motor current increases.

figure.purpose: Create the opening contradiction between unchanged e.m.f. and a lower loaded terminal reading.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch in two panels. Same 6.0 V battery, first with a high-resistance voltmeter only reading about 6.0 V, then driving one motor with a voltmeter across the battery reading less than 6.0 V. Sparse blue and red annotations. No formula or numerical answer.
figure.alt_text: The same battery has a higher terminal reading with almost no load than while driving a motor.

blocks.heading: A real source has an inside
content: A useful model places an ideal e.m.f. 𝓔 in series with an internal resistance r. The external load is R. The same current I passes through the source model and the single external load.

The source supplies 𝓔 joules to each coulomb. Inside the source, Ir joules per coulomb are transferred to thermal energy. The amount left for the external circuit is the terminal potential difference V.

figure.purpose: Make the physical and circuit-model locations of internal and external energy transfer visible.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper hand-drawn comparison. Left: a battery outline with an inner labelled r and outer lamp R. Right: its equivalent one-loop symbol model with ideal e.m.f. 𝓔, r and R in one path. Colour-code inside loss orange and external transfer blue.
figure.alt_text: A real battery is represented by an ideal e.m.f. in series with internal resistance and one external load.

blocks.heading: The terminal-p.d. relationship
content: Formula to remember: V = 𝓔 - Ir.
V is terminal potential difference in volts, 𝓔 is e.m.f. in volts, I is current in amperes and r is internal resistance in ohms. The product Ir is a potential difference in volts because A × Ω = V.
When current leaves the positive terminal and the source supplies energy, subtract the internal loss. This lesson uses only that discharging case.

figure.purpose: Show the per-coulomb energy account that gives the subtraction in the formula.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper energy-bar sketch for one coulomb. Full bar labelled 𝓔 J per C splits into an orange Ir J per C inside the source and a blue V J per C at the load. Beneath, show V = 𝓔 - Ir and A × Ω = V.
figure.alt_text: Source energy per coulomb splits into internal lost volts and terminal potential difference.

blocks.heading: Walkthrough: find the terminal p.d.
content: A field sensor draws 0.40 A from a source with e.m.f. 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω.
First find the inside transfer: Ir = 0.40 × 0.50 = 0.20 V.
Now carry that value into the terminal equation: V = 9.0 - 0.20 = 8.8 V.
Check the physics: 8.8 V is below 9.0 V because the source is delivering current. The unit check also works because A × Ω gives V.

figure.purpose: Model the complete calculation route with units and a physical check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated calculation layout with columns known, relationship, substitution and check. Use 𝓔 = 9.0 V, I = 0.40 A, r = 0.50 Ω, lost volts 0.20 V and terminal p.d. 8.8 V. Do not resemble a learner question.
figure.alt_text: A worked layout subtracts 0.20 V of lost volts from 9.0 V to obtain 8.8 V.

blocks.heading: Why a larger current gives a larger sag
content: Keep the same source, so 𝓔 and r stay fixed. If the external load draws more current, Ir becomes larger. More energy per coulomb is transferred inside the source, so V becomes smaller.
See it a second way. If the external load draws less current, the internal loss Ir shrinks. The terminal p.d. rises towards 𝓔. At I = 0, the model gives V = 𝓔.

It can feel as if the battery has less e.m.f. under load because the voltmeter reading falls. The e.m.f. belongs to the source energy supply per coulomb. The reading falls because a larger share is transferred inside the source.

figure.purpose: Contrast low-current and high-current energy shares and correct the changing-e.m.f. misconception.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-row comparison. Same 𝓔 and r in both rows. Low I has small orange Ir share and large blue V share; high I has larger orange Ir and smaller blue V. Add a crossed-out note saying e.m.f. changed and a correct note saying internal loss changed.
figure.alt_text: For the same source, higher current increases lost volts and lowers terminal potential difference.

blocks.heading: Walkthrough: work backward to internal resistance
content: A portable light uses one source. Its e.m.f. is 12.0 V, the current is 1.5 A and the measured terminal p.d. is 10.8 V.
The missing potential difference is 𝓔 - V = 12.0 - 10.8 = 1.2 V. This equals Ir.
Therefore r = (𝓔 - V)/I = 1.2/1.5 = 0.80 Ω.
Independent check: Ir = 1.5 × 0.80 = 1.2 V, and 10.8 + 1.2 returns to 12.0 V.

figure.purpose: Teach reverse solving and an independent reconstruction check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper reverse-flow calculation with arrows from 𝓔 and V to lost volts, then divide by I to obtain r. End with a separate reconstruction box V + Ir = 𝓔. Include all units.
figure.alt_text: A reverse calculation finds internal resistance from the difference between e.m.f. and terminal p.d.

blocks.heading: Source power and the boundary of this lesson
content: The source supplies electrical power P = 𝓔I. This is the electrical power produced by the source. If 𝓔 stays fixed and current increases, this source power increases.
The external load receives power VI. The internal resistance receives power I²r. These statements describe one source and one simple external load.
We have not used junction current rules, general loop equations or combined-resistance formulas. Those methods come later.

concepts_taught: source, external and internal power in a single-load circuit
misconceptions_addressed: The e.m.f. becomes smaller whenever terminal p.d. falls.
Terminal p.d. must equal e.m.f. while a real source supplies current.
next_lesson_can_assume: A real source can be modelled as e.m.f. in series with internal resistance.
For a discharging source, V = 𝓔 - Ir.
Increasing current at fixed e.m.f. and internal resistance increases lost volts and lowers terminal p.d.
Internal resistance can be found from r = (𝓔 - V)/I in a simple one-load circuit.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Kirchhoff's first law at a junction.
Kirchhoff's second law as a general method.
